title: Albert Cook's One-Year Trial: Opening Mengo Hospital in 1897
dek: In February 1897 the mission at Mengo let its new doctor practise medicine for a trial year; by May he had a ward.

story.founder: Albert Ruskin Cook, with Katharine Timpson (later Katharine Cook)
story.company: Mengo Hospital (Church Missionary Society medical mission, Kampala)
story.event: Starting medical work at Mengo on a one-year trial and opening the first wards
story.summary: Albert Cook, a Church Missionary Society doctor, reached Mengo, capital of Buganda, in February 1897 with a party that included the nurse Katharine Timpson. Colleagues who wanted him preaching instead agreed to a one-year trial of medical work; he began on 22 February in a dispensary shed, and the first reed-and-thatch ward of Mengo Hospital opened in mid-May. During Mwanga's revolt and the Sudanese mutiny that year he treated more than 150 bullet wounds, and the hospital grew to 75 beds by 1901.
paragraphs: On 19 February 1897, after a march of nearly three months from Mombasa, Albert Cook reached Mengo, the capital of the Buganda kingdom. The Church Missionary Society had sent him as a doctor with a party of twelve that included Katharine Timpson, a nurse trained at Guy's Hospital. Buganda was by then under a British protectorate, and the mission's main reason for posting a doctor there was to care for missionaries who fell ill.

The day after he arrived, the missionaries met. Many wanted Cook to take up preaching, leave the small dispensary to Miss Pilgrim, who already ran it from a shed, and send Timpson to Ngogwe, about thirty miles away. The caravan leader, Dr Baxter, argued against them, and the meeting agreed that Cook and Timpson could practise medicine at Mengo for one year, as a trial. Weeks later Archdeacon R. H. Walker told London he weighed medical work by "how far it is likely to aid our work not how much suffering will be relieved".

Cook began on 22 February in Pilgrim's shed. He judged there was "probably good scope for work", and he was soon seeing fifty to eighty patients a day. He obtained the Katikiro's promise of a hospital with wards for men and women. His plans came to about £300; Walker objected, noting that some Baganda Christians had been put off by deaths after operations, and the mission settled on a smaller building at £150 to £200. The first six-bed ward opened in mid-May, with reed walls, a thatched roof and a floor of stamped mud.

Treatment came with preaching. Each day began with prayers in the wards, and attending religious instruction was a condition of care; when Roman Catholics protested, Cook told them to take the Gospel with the medicine or go without the medicine. In July the Kabaka, Mwanga, fled Mengo and rose against the protectorate, and in September Sudanese troops mutinied. Within a few weeks Cook treated more than 150 bullet wounds, and Timpson led the mission's women in nursing the wounded.

The society counted 12,435 dispensary visits in nine months. Nobody ended the trial. The hospital had seventy-five beds by 1901, Cook and Timpson married in 1900, and Mengo Hospital still stands on Namirembe hill.

quote.text: like a beautiful flower, full of colour and full of scent, are the fine and fruitful words of him who acts accordingly.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: Cook's colleagues argued over whether healing was worth anything beyond the preaching it supported. The Dhammapada puts words and deeds the other way round: speech becomes fruitful when the speaker acts on it. At Mengo the trial was settled less by argument than by the patients who kept coming.

reflection: Cook did not win the argument on his second day in Mengo. He was given a year by colleagues who mostly saw his work as a means to something else, and he spent it doing the work where it could be seen: patients seen and counted, wards built at the price others would accept.

You may be on a trial of your own, with a funder, a colleague or someone at home who has not yet decided what your work is for. Arguing that case every week is tiring. Sometimes it is enough to agree the terms clearly, let the work be seen, and go home at a sensible hour.
invitation: If someone is waiting to see whether your work deserves their backing, write one sentence saying what they would need to see, and by when. Then leave that sentence alone until tomorrow.

cross_checks.claim: Cook began medical work at Mengo on 22 February 1897
Missionaries who wanted Cook preaching allowed medical work only on a one-year trial
The first ward opened in mid-May 1897 (15 May in Foster, 14 May in the DACB entries)
Cook and the nurse Katharine Timpson travelled in the CMS Uganda party of 1896
Mwanga's revolt and the Sudanese mutiny of 1897 brought large numbers of wounded to Cook
The dispensary saw many thousands of visits in the first year (12,435 in nine months by the CMS report; over 17,000 in the first year by Foster's count)

research_notes: Arrival: Foster (from the CMS and Mengo archives) says nine of the party crossed the lake and reached the port nearest Mengo on 15 February 1897, while Cook marched round by land and reached Mengo on 19 February; the DACB (Sempala) gives 19 February; the hospital's own history gives 15 February. The story uses 19 February for Cook. First clinic: Foster and the DACB say Cook began in a shed Miss Pilgrim already used as a dispensary; the hospital's own tradition says the first outpatient clinic, on 22 February, was held under a tree on Namirembe Hill. The story follows the archival account and keeps the shared date. First ward: Foster gives 15 May (a second six-bed ward on 24 May); both DACB entries give 14 May; the CMS annual report says the new hospital of men's and women's wards and operating room was dedicated in June. The story says the first ward opened in mid-May. Patient figures: the CMS report (1897-98) gives 12,435 dispensary visits, 186 in-patients and 196 operations in nine months; Foster, from the hospital records, gives over 17,000 dispensary patients and 189 admissions in the first year, but elsewhere 141 in-patients for 1897; the story uses only the society's contemporary nine-month dispensary figure. Bullet wounds: Foster says over 150 in a few weeks from August 1897; the CMS report dates Mwanga's flight from Mengo to 6 July. Katharine's name: Wellcome Collection and Foster's 'K. Timpson' support Katharine; the DACB and the hospital site spell it Katherine. She was not his wife in 1897; they married in 1900. Colonial context: the story states that Buganda was under a British protectorate, that the doctor's first purpose was to care for missionaries, that religious instruction was a condition of treatment (Foster, quoting Cook) and that Mwanga rose against the protectorate; it does not repeat the CMS report's contemporary judgements of Mwanga. Foster, writing in 1968, calls the condition an 'inhuman threat' and suggests it explains the government medical officer Robert Moffat's poor opinion of the CMS missionaries; the story reports the condition without comment. The Walker and Cook quotations are taken from Foster, who quotes their letters in the CMS archives. Cook added that the Roman Catholics chose to attend. The 1970 BMJ article by W. R. Billington could not be read (its PMC PDF sits behind a download check), so it is not cited. Foster's article was read in full from Cambridge's PDF; the landing page is cited.
